changes.before: Add labeled name, email, and activity fields with a submit button.
changes.after: Build a small signup form with clearly named fields.

before: A form collects related choices or information. The form element groups its controls. An input is a single entry field; a select offers choices; a button can submit the form. A label tells a person what a control asks for. Controls need meaningful names even before someone types anything. A placeholder inside a field disappears while typing and should not replace its label. HTML can ask the browser to catch simple missing or malformed values, but saving information needs additional behavior and another system to receive it.

This form fragment belongs inside body. It demonstrates a labeled required field.

```html
<form>
  <label for="visitor">Visitor name</label>
  <input id="visitor" name="visitor" type="text" required>

  <label for="contact">Contact email</label>
  <input id="contact" name="contact" type="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Request information</button>
</form>
```

The label's for value matches the input's id exactly. Clicking a label can move focus to its connected field. input is a void element and needs no closing tag. required is a Boolean attribute: its presence turns the requirement on. Do not write required="false" to turn it off; remove it instead.

id and name have different jobs. An id identifies one element on the page, so use a unique id for each control. A label's for points to that id. name supplies the field's key when a form sends values, such as contact=someone@example.org. Matching a label to a control does not require matching name, but submitted controls generally need name. Attribute values belong inside quotes, and settings go in the opening tag. Keep labels next to the fields they describe so the visual order also makes sense.

type="email" tells the browser to check the shape of an email address when the form is submitted. It may also offer an email-friendly keyboard. required tells the browser that the field cannot be blank. Together they cover different problems: empty input and an address with the wrong shape. They do not prove that an address exists or belongs to the person. A server, the system receiving submitted information, still needs its own validation. Client-side validation means checks in the browser; it helps people correct errors but can be bypassed.

This fragment is another form, using a list of choices. Put it in body to try it separately.

```html
<form>
  <label for="session">Choose a session</label>
  <select id="session" name="session">
    <option value="music">Music</option>
    <option value="clay">Clay modeling</option>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Choose session</button>
</form>
```

select contains option elements. Music is the visible option text; value="music" is the value sent if that option is selected. option and select use closing tags. The label connects to session just as it connects to an input. A submit button asks the browser to submit its form after eligible validation checks.

Try three kinds of input before trusting a form: missing, malformed, and valid. For a required email field, submit it empty, then enter a clearly malformed address, then an address-shaped example such as learner@example.org. Notice the different results. Native validation messages and appearance depend on the browser and its language. A form without a real receiving endpoint does not enroll someone or store their information. You can learn labeling and validation here without claiming that submission has connected to a registration service.

For this project, use controls with id="name", id="email", and id="activity", each connected to a visible label. Require name and email; set email's type to email. Use select with options for the activity and a submit button. Each label's for must exactly match its control's id. The checks find those relationships and attributes. Then try the blank and malformed cases yourself. Good form instructions should tell a person how to fix a problem without clearing their other answers or making them guess which field needs attention.
after: A form groups information someone can enter. Put its fields inside `<form>`. Give each field a visible `<label>` so people know what to type or choose. A hint inside an empty field can help, but it should not replace the label.

This form asks for a name.

```html
<form>
  <label for="visitor">Visitor name</label>
  <input id="visitor" name="visitor" type="text" required>
  <button type="submit">Request information</button>
</form>
```

The label’s `for` matches the input’s `id`. `type="text"` makes a text field. `required` means it cannot be left blank. The submit button asks the form to send its values.

`id` and `name` have different jobs. `id` gives one field a unique label on the page, which `for` can point to. `name` is the key used for that field’s value when the form sends data. Give each field both.

`type="email"` asks the browser to check that the entry looks like an email address. `required` also stops the field being left blank. These checks do not prove the address exists. To stop requiring a field, remove `required`; writing `required="false"` still turns it on.

A `<select>` lets someone choose from `<option>` items.

```html
<form>
  <label for="session">Choose a session</label>
  <select id="session" name="session">
    <option value="music">Music</option>
    <option value="clay">Clay modeling</option>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Choose session</button>
</form>
```

The label points to the select’s id. `Music` is the text people see. `value="music"` is the value sent for that choice. The button submits the form.

Try an email field with three entries: nothing, an address missing `@`, and `learner@example.org`. A required email field should reject the first two. Browser checks help people correct mistakes. They do not save a signup; that needs a receiving service.

Add name, email and activity fields with the ids `name`, `email` and `activity`. Give each a matching label and a `name` attribute. Require name and email. Use `type="email"` for email and a `<select>` with options for activity. Keep a submit button.

before: Add fields for name and email, plus a list for choosing an activity.
Give each field its own id. On its label, set for to that same id.
Add required to the name and email fields.
Set the email field to type="email".
Try submitting blank fields. Then try an email address with no @ sign.
after: Add labeled name and email inputs with required.
Add a labeled activity select with options.

before.question: A label has for="email", but its input has id="contact". What change connects this label to that input?
choices: Put both elements on the same line
Change only the input name to "email"
before.explanation: for must match the input id. The name controls the submitted key; visual placement does not create the association.

after.question: A label has for="email", but the input has id="contact". How can you connect them?
choices: Put them on the same line.
Change only the input’s name to "email".
after.explanation: A label’s `for` must match the field’s `id`. Its position and name do not make that connection.

before: Use required and type="email" on the named fields.
after: Each label’s `for` must match its field’s `id`.
Use `id="email" name="email" type="email" required` for email.
Give each option a value and readable text.

project.title: An activity signup form
project.task: Add labeled name, email and activity fields, plus a submit button.
project.done_when: Each field has a matching label and a name. Name and email are required, email uses type="email", and activity offers choices.
